summary: Extends IS-IS to support Traffic Engineering by defining new information that routers can put into link state packets. This describes additional details about the state of links, useful for traffic engineering computations such as choosing paths based on bandwidth. It replaced RFC 3784 and has been updated later.

eli5.summary: Roads carry traffic better if planners know which are busy. This lets routers also share extra facts about each link, like free room, so paths can be chosen with traffic in mind.

questions: what is tlv type 22 in is-is
what is the up down bit in is-is
subtitle: New IS-IS building blocks that let routers advertise link details such as bandwidth, plus wider metrics and a loop-proof way to leak prefixes down levels.

tldr.problem: Plain IS-IS only carries a 6-bit link metric (0-63) and little else about a link, which is not enough for traffic engineering computations such as choosing paths by available bandwidth.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the extended IS reachability TLV (type 22) with a 24-bit metric and nested sub-TLVs for link details, the extended IP reachability TLV (type 135) with a 32-bit metric and an up/down bit, and a router ID TLV (type 134).
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 3784 and moves the specification to the standards track. It has since been updated by RFC 5307 and RFC 8918.

today: RFC 5305 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 3784 and has been updated by RFC 5307 and RFC 8918.

sections.title: Why IS-IS Needed New TLVs
sections.content:
IS-IS routers each advertise Link State Protocol Data Units (LSPs). An LSP is a fixed header followed by TLVs: tuples of a Type, a Length and a Value. TLVs make the format flexible and extensible.

RFC 5305 designs new TLVs that replace the existing IS Neighbor TLV and IP Reachability TLV and add information about the characteristics of a link. Those characteristics are needed for traffic engineering, as described in RFC 2702. Secondary goals are a larger dynamic range for the IS-IS metric and a better encoding of IP prefixes.

The RFC does not discuss how to migrate to the new TLVs. It is a standards track version of the earlier Informational RFC 3784.
sections.eli5: Routers send each other little labeled notes. This document invents new kinds of notes that can hold more details about each road between routers.

sections.title: Sub-TLVs: TLVs Inside TLVs
sections.content:
The RFC introduces the sub-TLV. TLVs live inside IS-IS packets; sub-TLVs live inside TLVs and add extra information to one particular TLV. Each sub-TLV has a one-octet Type, a one-octet Length and zero or more octets of Value.

A receiver must ignore and skip sub-TLVs it does not know. The sub-TLV type space is managed by the IETF IS-IS working group. New values are allocated after review on its mailing list, which normally requires documentation of how the new type is used. If the working group has disbanded, a Designated Expert assigned by the responsible Area Director does the review.
sections.eli5: It is like a labeled envelope that can hold smaller labeled envelopes. If you find an envelope you do not understand, you just skip it.

sections.title: The Extended IS Reachability TLV
sections.content:
TLV type 22 describes a router's neighbors. The old IS reachability TLV (type 2) used one octet for the default metric, leaving 6 bits for the value, so metrics ran from 0 to 63. It also carried delay, monetary cost and reliability metrics that are not commonly implemented.

Each neighbor entry in the new TLV holds 7 octets of system ID and pseudonode number, 3 octets of default metric, 1 octet giving the length of the sub-TLVs, and 0 to 244 octets of sub-TLVs. With no sub-TLVs an entry takes 11 octets, so one TLV can describe up to 23 neighbors.

The metric is a 24-bit unsigned integer, whereas the metric in the extended IP reachability TLV is 32 bits, so that an intra-area route cost is very unlikely to be cut off when used in an inter-area route. To avoid overflow in a traffic engineering SPF (Shortest Path First) calculation, any metric at or above MAX_PATH_METRIC is treated as MAX_PATH_METRIC, which is 4,261,412,864 (0xFE000000). A link advertised with the maximum link metric (2^24 - 1) MUST NOT be used in the normal SPF computation. That lets a link be advertised for traffic engineering without being used for hop-by-hop routing.
sections.eli5: Each road between routers gets a bigger price tag, so it can say 'very expensive' with far more precision. A road with the highest tag is kept off the everyday map but can still be used for special trips.

sections.title: The Link Sub-TLVs
sections.content:
Seven sub-TLVs are established for the extended IS reachability TLV. Unless stated otherwise, multiple occurrences of the information are carried by repeating the sub-TLV.

  • Administrative group (type 3): a 4-octet bit mask set by the administrator. Each set bit is one group assigned to the interface. The least significant bit is 'group 0' and the most significant is 'group 31'.
  • IPv4 interface address (type 6) and IPv4 neighbor address (type 8): 4-octet addresses. Implementations MUST NOT inject a /32 prefix for them into their routing or forwarding table, because that can cause forwarding loops with systems that do not support the sub-TLV.
  • Maximum link bandwidth (type 9) and maximum reservable link bandwidth (type 10): each is a 32-bit IEEE floating point number in bytes (not bits) per second. The reservable figure can exceed the link's bandwidth for oversubscription.
  • Unreserved bandwidth (type 11): eight 32-bit floating point numbers, one for each setup priority 0 through 7, with priority 0 first. Rapid changes in these values SHOULD NOT cause rapid generation of LSPs.
  • TE default metric (type 18): a 24-bit administratively assigned metric that gives traffic engineering SPF a differently weighted topology. Without it, the normal default metric of the link MUST be used.

A router that implements traffic engineering MUST include the IPv4 interface address sub-TLV, and MUST include the neighbor address sub-TLV on point-to-point adjacencies. The bandwidth, administrative group and TE metric sub-TLVs are optional and SHOULD appear at most once per TLV.
sections.eli5: Each road can carry sticky notes: its color group, the addresses at each end, how wide it is, how much room is still free for each priority level, and an alternate price just for planners.

sections.title: The Extended IP Reachability TLV
sections.content:
TLV type 135 carries IP prefixes. The old IP reachability TLVs (types 128 and 130, from RFC 1195) had the same 0-63 metric limit and allowed prefixes to be advertised only upward in the level hierarchy. The new TLV gives a 32-bit metric and one bit to show that a prefix has been redistributed down.

Each entry has 4 octets of metric, 1 control octet (1 up/down bit, 1 bit saying sub-TLVs are present, 6 bits of prefix length), 0 to 4 octets of IPv4 prefix, and optional sub-TLVs. Prefix length runs from 0 to 32, and the prefix is sent in the fewest octets that hold that many significant bits: 0 bits take 0 octets, 1-8 take 1, 9-16 take 2, 17-24 take 3 and 25-32 take 4. Leftover bits are sent as zero and ignored on receipt.

A prefix with a metric larger than MAX_PATH_METRIC MUST NOT be considered in normal SPF computation, so it can be advertised for other purposes. The RFC defines no sub-TLVs for this TLV; the practical maximum for them is 250 octets.
sections.eli5: This is the address list. Each address says how many digits really matter, and only that many are sent, which saves space.

sections.title: The Up/Down Bit and the Router ID
sections.content:
If routers could freely pass prefixes between level 1 and level 2, a prefix learned via level 2 and advertised down into level 1 might be advertised back up, creating a routing loop if the original source withdraws it. RFC 1195 avoided this by allowing only upward advertisement.

The up/down bit fixes this. It is 0 when a prefix is first injected into IS-IS. When a prefix is advertised from a higher level to a lower one, such as level 2 to level 1, the bit MUST be set to 1, and prefixes with the bit set may only be advertised down. The bit is also set to 1 when a prefix moves between areas at the same level. Its semantics are identical to the up/down bit in RFC 5302.

The Traffic Engineering router ID TLV (type 134) holds the 4-octet router ID of the originating router, a single stable address that can always be referenced in a path, whatever the state of the node's interfaces. A router that implements traffic engineering MUST include it, and it SHOULD NOT appear more than once in an LSP. If the router advertises BGP prefixes with the BGP next hop set to the BGP router ID, the TE router ID SHOULD be the same. Implementations MUST NOT inject a /32 prefix for it into the forwarding table.
sections.eli5: A little arrow on each address note says whether it has already traveled down from the big highway to the small streets. Notes with the arrow only go down, so they never loop back. Each router also gets one permanent name tag.

sections.title: IANA Registries
sections.content:
Three TLV types are recorded: 22 (extended IS reachability), 134 (Traffic Engineering router ID) and 135 (extended IP reachability). All three appear in LSPs and not in IIH or SNP packets.

Two new registries are created, one for sub-TLVs of TLV 22 and one for sub-TLVs of TLV 135, each with values 0 to 255. Allocation requires documentation of the proposed use and approval by the Designated Expert assigned by the IESG. The TLV 22 registry is initialized with the sub-TLVs defined here plus others such as 4 (Link Local/Remote Identifiers), 19 (Link-attributes) and 22 (Bandwidth Constraints), with 250-254 reserved for Cisco specific extensions and 255 for future expansion. No codepoints are defined for the TLV 135 registry.
sections.eli5: A central list records which note-type numbers mean what, so nobody reuses a number for something else.

sections.title: Security
sections.content: The RFC states that it raises no new security issues for IS-IS. For general IS-IS security considerations it points to RFC 5304, which covers IS-IS cryptographic authentication.
sections.eli5: These new notes are no more risky than the old ones, so the existing lock on the mailbox is the protection.
